problem: Prior multi-robot LLM/learning-based path planning needs large-scale training, prior maps or scene models, or simulation, so it transfers poorly to real, dynamic, unknown environments where the target is out of sight.
motivation: Heterogeneous robots have complementary strengths (a valuable but slow humanoid and a cheap, agile quadruped). Letting the cheap scout explore for the valuable agent could allow real-world deployment without training, priors or simulation. Landmark-sparse and obstacle-rich spaces are the hard cases.
key_idea: A coordinator-explorer scheme in which a humanoid (Unitree G1) delegates waypoint scouting to a quadruped (Unitree Go2), with both guided by a zero-shot multimodal LLM and two adaptive exploration modes (X for landmark-sparse scenes, Y for obstacle-rich scenes).
insight: The ablations show the modes address different failures. Removing Mode X cuts quadruped command compliance from 86% to 56.27% and raises revisits and redundant rotations. Removing Mode Y makes obstacle avoidance collapse (V_avoid 0.23, no time reported). A humanoid-only setup fails in scenes 3 and 4 (CR 33.33% and 40.00% vs 100%), so the embodiment split matters. Against two human operators the system is slower and less precise in the harder scenes, so parity with humans is only partial.
method: Coordinator-explorer architecture: the humanoid handles task coordination and goal reaching, while the quadruped explores and reports feasible paths or intermediate waypoints.

Humanoid pipeline: a loop of path evaluation (is the target visible and reachable from I_B), pilot exploration (assign waypoints L_W to the quadruped and keep only informative ones), and task execution with continuous re-evaluation.

Quadruped pipeline (Algorithm 1): 360° scan to check waypoint visibility, move to the waypoint, 360° scan for the target L_T and path feasibility, then report success or failure with perception data to the humanoid.
Mode X (landmark-sparse): extensive repositioning and panoramic scanning to maximize target visibility and reduce redundant exploration from perceptual aliasing.

Mode Y (obstacle-rich): an extra scan within a half-angle R_scan (π/2) to find passages or corridors, allowing temporary deviation from the goal direction; the mode is chosen by an accessibility check on I_D.
Perception and decision-making with Doubao-vision-3.6 VLM, used zero-shot with limits d_max=2 m per turn, R_max=π/2 rad and a success threshold of 0.5 m.

setting.observation: egocentric first-person visual streams from the humanoid (I_B) and the quadruped (I_D)
setting.action_space: high-level natural-language waypoints and motion commands (up to 2 m displacement, up to π/2 rad rotation per turn) executed by the robots' own controllers

numbers_note: Paper reports per-scene results on a self-made 5-scene real-world benchmark; only three of the five scenes are listed as numbers entries, the others are in tables. Scenes 2 and 3 are in the tables but were omitted here. Ablation on Mode Y: G1-Go2 Time 154.89, V_avoid 1.00; no-Y V_avoid 0.23.
results: On five real-world scenes TZPP completes all tasks (CR 100%) and is near human in path length (D e.g. 4.00 vs 3.80 m, 6.80 vs 6.47 m), but it is slower and less precise in harder scenes (scene 5 time 154.89 s vs 94.21 s; RMSE higher). It beats the G1-only ablation, which fails on scenes 3 and 4 (CR 33.33% and 40.00%).
limitations: Small, self-designed real-world evaluation (5 scenes, two human participants) with no comparison to existing methods
Noticeably slower than humans in complex scenes (long time, large rotation, higher RMSE) and no quantitative success or SPL benchmarks
Dependence on a proprietary VLM (Doubao-vision-3.6) and hand-designed mode logic; the paper reports no per-trial variance
